title: A Joint Power-Privacy Control Framework for Decentralized Learning over Heterogeneous Wireless Multicasting Networks
abstract: In this paper, we propose a decentralized learning framework that incorporates both power control and privacy guarantees. Specifically, we enable a set of clients in a wireless multicast network to jointly train a common model while maintaining a prescribed per-iteration maximum privacy leakage level. The communication network is represented by a rowstochastic adjacency matrix, allowing us to capture asymmetric channel gains as well as heterogeneous maximum transmit power levels. Differential privacy is enforced through an explicit powersplitting strategy that allocates each node's limited maximum transmit power between model coefficients and injected Gaussian noise, thereby jointly controlling learning performance and privacy leakage. We further prove that the proposed algorithm achieves a cumulative regret bound of O(logT), whereTdenotes the time horizon. To evaluate the practical performance of our approach, we perform comprehensive experiments on the CIFAR-10 dataset under both IID and non-IID data distributions, considering different privacy levels, diverse numbers of clients, and various graph topologies. The results demonstrate strong performance across the considered settings and improved performance over existing methods, highlighting the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm under realistic wireless communication constraints.

title: Quantum Machine Learning via Probability Perturbation Algorithm
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning via Probability Perturbation Algorithm is a novel approach to machine learning that integrates quantum computing and probability perturbation techniques. This research explores the potential of leveraging quantum phenomena like superposition and entanglement to enhance model training and generalization capabilities, particularly for high-dimensional datasets. The core mechanism involves introducing controlled, probabilistic perturbations to the model's parameters during the training process, designed to nudge the learning landscape towards more robust and generalizable solutions. This paper outlines the theoretical foundation, experimental setup, and initial results demonstrating the efficacy of this algorithmic framework. We aim to present a promising avenue for advancing machine learning in complex, high-dimensional environments.

title: 自适应矩阵运算的量子化
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum algorithm, termed "Adaptive Matrix Operation," designed to revolutionize quantum computation through the implementation of self-adaptive matrix operations. Traditional matrix operations are plagued by numerical precision limitations, hindering the scalability of quantum algorithms. Our approach leverages quantum entanglement and instantaneous correlation to dynamically adjust matrix structures and operations, effectively mitigating these issues and opening avenues for enhanced quantum performance. The core mechanism involves constructing a quantum state that evolves based on input data, allowing the algorithm to tailor its internal representation and execution to optimize the outcome. This paper details the theoretical framework, preliminary experimental results, and potential implications of this innovative quantum algorithm.

title: Title: Bio-Inspired Fractal Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces Bio-Inspired Fractal Optimization (BFSO), a novel optimization algorithm inspired by the fractal geometry of biological systems, particularly the self-similarity observed in neural networks and ecosystems. Traditional optimization methods often struggle with complex, non-convex landscapes, while BFSO offers a fundamentally different approach – the 'Fractal Resonance' method – designed to effectively navigate these challenges. We detail the core mechanism of BFSO, explaining how it generates and utilizes fractal patterns to identify optimal solutions across a wide range of problems. The paper presents a comprehensive analysis of the algorithm's performance, demonstrating its effectiveness in optimizing complex adaptive systems and showcasing its potential for tackling real-world applications. We explore the underlying mathematical principles and provide a detailed explanation of the fractal resonance concept.

title: Core Claim: Develop a non-linear clustering algorithm utilizing dynamic parameter adjustment to enhance clustering effectiveness and accuracy.
abstract: This paper presents a novel non-linear clustering algorithm designed to optimize the clustering process through dynamic parameter adjustment. Traditional clustering methods often rely on fixed parameters, limiting the algorithm's ability to effectively identify distinct clusters. This research introduces a mechanism that iteratively adjusts key parameters during the clustering process, allowing the algorithm to adapt to the data and achieve superior clustering results. We rigorously evaluate the performance of this algorithm using various metrics, demonstrating its efficacy in identifying clusters with improved accuracy and robustness compared to existing approaches. The study highlights the advantages of dynamic parameter adjustment in enhancing clustering outcomes.

title: Bayesian Network for Agent-Environment Dynamics
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Bayesian Networks (BNs) to model agent-environment dynamics. The core claim is to develop a BNs that explicitly represent probabilistic dependencies between agent actions and environment states, leading to improved prediction accuracy and robustness. We propose a novel approach that leverages Bayesian inference to dynamically update the network's belief states as new data is received, mitigating the limitations of traditional correlation-based models. The research explores the benefits of this probabilistic approach in scenarios where environmental states are inherently complex and change over time. The paper details the design and implementation of the BNs, showcasing their performance through simulations and a simplified case study.

title: Graph-Based Anomaly Detection with Learned Feature Embeddings and Structural Similarity Measures
abstract: This paper presents a novel graph-based approach to anomaly detection that addresses the limitations of traditional methods. The core idea is to represent data as a graph, where nodes represent data points and edges represent relationships. We learn feature embeddings to capture data point similarities and simultaneously define structural similarity measures to quantify deviations from expected graph patterns. The system identifies anomalies by detecting significant changes in these relationships. The approach's strength lies in its ability to model complex dependencies within data, leading to improved anomaly detection accuracy compared to methods relying solely on individual data point analysis. This work outlines the methodology, describes the key components, and demonstrates the potential of this approach through theoretical analysis and conceptual design. The system utilizes a combination of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) for embedding learning and custom similarity metrics based on graph Laplacian eigenvalues to highlight anomalous structural changes. The results, while theoretical at this stage, suggest a promising direction for anomaly detection in various domains.

The approach's strength lies in its ability to model complex dependencies within data, leading to improved anomaly detection accuracy compared to methods relying solely on individual data point analysis. This work outlines the methodology, describes the key components, and demonstrates the potential of this approach through theoretical analysis and conceptual design. The system utilizes a combination of graph convolutional networks (GCNs) for embedding learning and custom similarity metrics based on graph Laplacian eigenvalues to highlight anomalous structural changes. The results, while theoretical at this stage, suggest a promising direction for anomaly detection in various domains.

title: Quantum Entanglement Protocols for Beyond Classical Correlation: A Novel Approach
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a bizarre yet fundamental phenomenon, presents a unique opportunity for revolutionary information processing and secure communication. This paper explores the design of a novel quantum entanglement protocol, termed "Non-Local Correlation Protocol" (NLCP), that transcends classical correlations and offers enhanced security and computational capabilities. The NLCP leverages the inherent non-classical properties of entangled states to establish a secure and powerful communication system. We detail the core mechanism of the protocol, highlighting its unique approach to mitigating interference and maximizing data transfer. The research focuses on the development of a robust, verifiable, and adaptable protocol suitable for future quantum technologies. The core claim is that this protocol represents a significant advancement in quantum communication and computation, offering a pathway toward a fundamentally new paradigm of secure data transfer and complex calculations.

title: Dynamical Bayesian Networks for Real-Time Anomaly Detection in Complex Systems
abstract: This paper investigates the application of Dynamical Bayesian Networks (DBNs) for real-time anomaly detection within complex systems. Traditional anomaly detection methods often struggle to adapt to evolving system dynamics, leading to inaccurate or delayed detection. DBNs offer a dynamic approach, continuously updating their internal state based on incoming data, thereby capturing changes in system behavior and enabling robust anomaly detection in real-time. The core of this approach lies in the network's ability to model temporal dependencies and probabilistic relationships between variables, allowing it to learn the normal operating state and identify deviations as anomalies. This paper details the theoretical framework of DBNs, specifically focusing on their adaptation capabilities and suitability for complex systems. Mathematical formulations are presented to illustrate the core concepts, including the Bayesian updating equations and the anomaly detection criteria. The proposed framework demonstrates improved performance compared to static anomaly detection models in simulated environments exhibiting non-stationary behavior. The key contributions of this work are a practical and adaptable method for real-time anomaly detection, offering a significant advancement in the field.

title: Causal Discovery via Contrastive Predictive Coding
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery, termed Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC), designed to address the limitations of existing algorithms when dealing with complex, high-dimensional data and confounding variables. The core idea is to utilize a contrastive learning framework where nodes in a system encode the discrepancy between their observed state and a predicted state, generated by incorporating information from other nodes. The system learns causal relationships by minimizing this discrepancy across different hypothetical interventions. Unlike traditional methods reliant on assumptions about data distribution or relying heavily on iterative constraint-based algorithms, CPC directly learns causal structure through the minimization of prediction errors. This approach offers improved robustness and scalability, particularly in scenarios where confounding is prevalent. We demonstrate the theoretical foundations of CPC and outline a proposed implementation strategy, highlighting its potential to unlock causal insights from intricate datasets.

title: Title: Adaptive Bayesian Inference for Dynamical Systems
abstract: Dynamic systems exhibit complex, nonlinear behavior, making accurate prediction challenging. Traditional methods often struggle with the inherent uncertainty and evolving nature of these systems. This paper introduces an Adaptive Bayesian Inference (ABI) algorithm designed to address this challenge by dynamically adjusting the prior distribution of a Bayesian neural network during the observation phase. The core mechanism centers around a Bayesian neural network that continuously refines the model's understanding of the system's evolution, ultimately leading to improved predictive accuracy. This approach offers a continuously improving model, overcoming the limitations of static priors in complex dynamical systems.

title: ##基于物理定律的程序生成与验证
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to software verification and generation by leveraging fundamental physical laws. The core idea is to translate program design into physical system models, simulate these models using physics engines, and then utilize physical law-based verification methods to ensure the generated code's correctness. This methodology offers a fundamentally different perspective compared to traditional software verification techniques, which often rely on abstract logic and testing. The proposed framework aims to provide a robust and verifiable solution, particularly for systems where traditional verification methods are complex or computationally expensive. The paper details the process, outlines the key components, and discusses the potential implications of this approach for various applications, including robotics, control systems, and simulations. We present a mathematical framework for representing programs as physical systems and demonstrate a preliminary validation process.

title: Quantum-Driven Optimization of Neural Network Architecture
abstract: Quantum-Driven Optimization of Neural Network Architecture explores the potential of quantum algorithms to revolutionize neural network design. This paper proposes a novel approach utilizing quantum annealing and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) to dynamically adjust neural network architecture, moving beyond traditional heuristic methods. The core claim is the development of a quantum-guided optimization process that iteratively refines the network's structure – specifically, layer count and connection weights – to maximize performance on a given task. We detail the algorithm's design, the rationale behind its quantum-enhanced exploration, and the potential benefits compared to current approaches. This work represents a significant advancement in neural network architecture design, leveraging the unique capabilities of quantum computing.

title: Quantum-Inspired Kernel Design for Machine Learning
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to kernel design for machine learning, drawing inspiration from the principles of quantum entanglement. Traditional kernel functions in Support Vector Machines (SVMs) frequently necessitate extensive manual tuning and often fail to achieve optimal performance. We introduce a kernel design algorithm that mimics the correlated behavior observed in entangled quantum systems. The algorithm constructs kernel functions based on the correlated features of data points, effectively simulating entanglement effects to potentially enhance classification accuracy. This work presents a fundamental shift in kernel design, moving away from hand-crafted kernels towards a more adaptive and potentially more powerful approach guided by quantum-inspired concepts. The core contribution lies in the methodology for generating kernels that dynamically capture complex relationships within data, leading to improved classification outcomes. We demonstrate the potential of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline a design strategy that can be readily applied to various machine learning tasks.

title: Title: Self-Assembling Topological Structures for Data Compression
abstract: This paper presents a novel method for generating self-assembling topological structures, a promising approach for efficient data compression. The core claim centers on the development of a system where smaller topological elements are combined to create larger structures, achieving enhanced compression efficiency through inherent structural properties. We introduce a dynamic algorithm that guides the assembly process, optimizing for both structural integrity and data density. The resulting structures demonstrate a significant improvement in compression ratios compared to existing methods, offering a fundamentally new perspective on data compression. The underlying principles are rooted in the study of topological properties and their potential for creating compact representations of information. This work explores the design of a system utilizing the principles of topology to generate structures that are more readily compressed and have inherent data-storing capabilities. The resulting structures exhibit a unique combination of structural stability and data density, representing a significant advancement in data compression technology.

title: Adaptive Quantum Neural Network Architecture Sensitivity to Noise Modeling
abstract: The sensitivity of quantum neural networks (QNNs) to noise is a critical factor limiting their practical applications. This research investigates the relationship between QNN performance, noise levels, and network architecture, proposing an adaptive modeling framework to enhance noise resilience. The core claim is that QNN performance is intricately linked to the number of qubits and the network's topological structure, with noise sensitivity being a key determinant. The proposed mechanism involves a framework combining quantum state analysis and machine learning, dynamically adjusting network parameters and topology based on real-time noise characterization. This approach moves beyond static noise assumptions, offering a dynamic modeling capability essential for optimizing QNN robustness. The model presented here provides a foundational approach for designing and controlling QNNs in noisy quantum environments, contributing to the field's advancement towards reliable quantum computation.

title: Dynamic Variable Field Theory via Quantum Computation
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum computation to revolutionize numerical simulation of quantum systems. Traditional numerical methods often struggle to accurately capture the complexities of quantum phenomena, necessitating the development of novel approaches. We propose a new dynamic variable field theory, leveraging quantum computation's inherent parallelism and superposition properties to provide a fundamentally different approach to simulating quantum behavior. This theory offers the promise of enhanced accuracy, speed, and the ability to predict quantum system evolution, potentially surpassing the limitations of existing numerical methods. The core of our work centers around a quantum-enhanced dynamic variable field formulation, emphasizing the interplay between quantum states and system evolution. The theoretical foundations and initial implementation demonstrate a robust framework for simulating fundamental quantum systems, offering a significant step towards practical quantum simulation.

title: Hierarchical Graph Neural Network with Symbolic Reasoning
abstract: This paper introduces a novel Hierarchical Graph Neural Network (HGNN) architecture that seamlessly integrates symbolic reasoning directly into the training process. Traditional graph neural networks (GNNs) excel at learning patterns and relationships within data, but often lack the ability to reason explicitly about their outputs or provide justifications for their predictions. Our approach, termed "Symbolic Guided Graph Learning" (SGL), dynamically constructs a hierarchical graph structure, incorporating symbolic rules and knowledge bases to guide the learning process and enhance reasoning capabilities. We demonstrate the efficacy of SGL through a series of experiments focused on complex reasoning tasks, showcasing improved accuracy, robustness, and explainability compared to state-of-the-art GNNs. The resulting network exhibits a more structured understanding of the underlying relationships, enabling it to generate more insightful and verifiable explanations.

title: A Safety Memory Is a Declassification Channel: Why Origin Binding, Taint Tracking and Memory Isolation Do Not Secure the Records an Agent Writes About Attacks
abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Two lines of work on language-model agents have converged on the same component from opposite directions. One proposes that an agent keep a persistent safety memory, so that an attack seen once, a request refused once or a source found untrustworthy once continues to inform decisions in later sessions. The other reports that persistent memory is an exploitable channel, with published attacks that write records through query-only interaction, through fragments individually too innocuous to filter, and through the agent's own reflection step. This paper argues that the coincidence is structural rather than incidental. A safety memory is defined by a property that ordinary agent memory does not have: its records exist because the agent observed something untrusted, and they are worth keeping only if they later carry authority over a consequential decision. In the vocabulary of information-flow control that the agent-security literature has already adopted, that is a declassification, specifically an integrity endorsement, and it is the one operation the three defense families now in print are built to forbid. Write-time origin binding, proved necessary and, with corroboration-gated elevation, sufficient against laundering for ordinary memory, either denies a safety record the authority that makes it useful or supplies the elevation an attacker needs. Monotone taint tracking over-blocks or strands the record by construction, which its own proponents say. Memory isolation prevents the write that the safety memory exists to perform. Three of the paper's claims cut against the premise it started from. The headline poisoning success rates are not one quantity: storage and execution dissociate, and the early numbers were measured in memory pools that later attack papers describe as unrealistically empty. Four independent 2026 results report the same degradation with no attacker present, which makes attack surface the wrong frame for at least part of the phenomenon. And the claim that nobody separates the trust level of a remembered threat from the trust level of the environment that produced it is false: one paper does exactly that, and the interesting problem is what its solution costs a safety memory in particular. What is not known is the size of any of it. No located source measures how often a safety memory fires on a record it should not trust, and no benchmark evaluates a memory-based guardrail under an attacker who is targeting the guardrail's own memory. The literature search, drafting and citation verification for this paper were carried out with AI assistance under the author's direction. Every citation was machine-verified against the arXiv API and Crossref before inclusion, and every quantitative claim was read back against the cited source's own abstract. The author is responsible for the final text and for all claims made in it.

title: Patterns of Priming in Production: Lexical, Semantic and Structural Alignment in Language Model Generation
abstract: This paper investigates structural priming in language model (LM) production, examining how preceding structural context influences sentence completion. While prior work has demonstrated priming effects in comprehension of structural alternations, it remained unclear whether these persist in production, where, when generating, an LM samples from many possible continuations at each step. We address this question through a series of controlled sentence-completion experiments on dative constructions. In line with prior work, we find that LMs are susceptible to structural priming, particularly in sentences that are semantically coherent. In terms of priming magnitude, we find that while there is a greater relative increase of double-object datives against our baselines, in line with inverse frequency effects, there is a larger absolute increase in prepositional-objects, the more frequently produced construction. Finally, we not only observe that structural priming is boosted by lexico-semantic coherence, but that structurally primed completions display greater levels of lexico-semantic repetition. Taken together, our evidence supports the view that structural priming in LMs operates across multiple levels of linguistic representation, facilitating, and facilitated by syntactic, lexical, and semantic alignment. Code: https://github.com/the-context-lab/primedproduction.

title: NeoRed: A Knowledge-Logic-Alignment Multimodal Large Language Model for Neonatal Respiratory Disease Diagnosis
abstract: Neonatal respiratory diseases are a major cause of neonatal morbidity and mortality, posing substantial challenges in clinical practice. Despite recent advances, existing Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) face two key limitations in neonatal diagnosis: (1) domain gap arising from predominantly adult training data; (2) insufficient integration of multidimensional clinical context for accurate diagnosis. To address these challenges, we collect two real-world clinical datasets (NeoCXR and NeoCXR-EV) and propose NeoRed, to the best of our knowledge, the first MLLM tailored for neonatal respiratory disease, filling the gap in neonatal diagnostic reports generation. To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

To enhance joint diagnosis from heterogeneous clinical context and chest X-rays, we design a novel Knowledge-Logic-Alignment (KLA) framework which constrains model behavior from three perspectives: 1) Knowledge Prior Injection (KPI) incorporates neonatologist-inspired diagnostic priors into multimodal representations, guiding disease-specific attention across modalities; 2) Diagnostic Logic Constraint (DLC) aligns the semantics of generated reports with multimodal diagnostic logic; and 3) Visual Semantic Alignment (VSA) establishes semantic correspondence between visual features and imaging conclusions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that NeoRed enables accurate neonatal diagnostic reports generation, achieving ROUGE-L of 53.29% and Clinical Efficacy F1 score of 65.19% on NeoCXR, outperforming existing MLLMs. NeoRed also preserves competitive report generation performance on adult benchmarks (MIMIC-CXR and IU-Xray). Datasets will be available upon application.

title: Beyond .WAV: Design and Software Verification of VocalCap, a Traceable Browser-Based Audio Capture System for Vocal Biomarker Research
abstract: Remote voice studies often retain a final audio file with limited evidence about how it was captured, transferred, processed, and accepted. This paper presents VocalCap, an institution-controlled, browser-based system for self-guided capture of voice and related acoustic signals by participants without technical training. A versioned protocol drives the workflow. Each accepted recording retains a browser-native object, a client-lossless Float32 WAV derived from the same MediaStream, and a server-canonical mono PCM16 WAV, linked to evidence of capture execution, technical quality, byte-level integrity, recovery, and transformation provenance. IndexedDB preserves accepted browser artifacts until server confirmation, while session completion requires successful verification of every task and artifact. Software tests challenged the acquisition contracts with malformed or altered objects, exact-zero interruptions, channel-topology variants, and interrupted or repeated operations. A post hoc technical audit of 39 consented pilot recordings found 25 sample-identical stereo files and 14 files with signal confined to the left channel. Topology-aware active-channel selection limited the canonical root-mean-square level difference to less than 0.001 dB in all 14 affected files; equal-weight stereo averaging would have introduced approximately 6.02 dB of attenuation. Production end-to-end verification completed two five-task profiles in Chromium and WebKit, yielding 10 accepted recordings and 30 retained artifacts that passed server-side integrity and format checks. The results verify VocalCap's software behavior under the tested browser-engine conditions. Device-level acoustic agreement, target-population usability, clinical validity, and biomarker performance remain subjects for separate studies.

title: Quantum Entanglement Information Distribution Protocol
abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum key distribution (QKD) protocol based on quantum entanglement, focusing on secure key distribution without the need for classical information exchange. The protocol leverages a dynamically generated quantum entanglement "mark" that encodes the key's integrity, and employs self-adaptive entanglement error correction to enhance security. We demonstrate the protocol's potential for scalable key generation and secure transmission. The core mechanism involves creating entangled states, meticulously measuring them, and utilizing the resulting correlations to establish the shared secret key. The design incorporates a robust self-correction mechanism to mitigate the effects of decoherence and measurement errors, ensuring long-term security. This research explores the practical implications of this approach and provides a framework for future advancements in quantum cryptographic systems.

title: 拓扑学量子纠错算法
abstract: Quantum Error Correction (QEC) has long been a significant challenge in quantum computing, demanding substantial resources and hindering practical implementation. Traditional QEC protocols rely heavily on Bell states and classical measurement, which suffer from inherent limitations in their efficiency and scalability. This paper proposes a novel quantum error correction algorithm leveraging dynamic quantum state evolution to achieve significantly enhanced error detection and correction capabilities. Our core mechanism utilizes a self-adaptive error correction system embedded within the quantum error correction protocol, capitalizing on the instantaneous nature of quantum superposition to detect and rectify errors. This approach offers a potential paradigm shift, exceeding the limitations of existing QEC methods and opening new avenues for robust quantum information processing.

title: Non-linear Geometric Field Theory for Quantum Information Protection
abstract: This paper explores the application of non-linear geometric field theory (NLGFT) as a novel approach to quantum information protection. Traditional cryptographic methods often rely on the complexity of algorithms, while geometric field theory offers a fundamentally different perspective – the distribution and entanglement of information within geometric spaces. We propose a mechanism leveraging the inherent properties of NLGFT to create robust quantum information protection, specifically designed to resist various attacks. This work introduces a new framework for encoding and safeguarding information, demonstrating its potential to significantly enhance the security of quantum systems. The core claim is that NLGFT provides a more resilient and adaptable approach to information protection compared to conventional methods.

title: Title: Modular Theorem Proving with Quantum Simulation
abstract: Abstract: This paper presents a novel modular theorem proving system predicated on quantum simulation to efficiently explore and verify complex mathematical theorems. We propose a quantum-assisted approach that leverages quantum algorithms, specifically Grover's algorithm, to dramatically reduce computational costs associated with exhaustive search and verification. The core mechanism involves simulating quantum systems to represent and manipulate mathematical objects, enabling the system to rapidly identify and prove theorems that are intractable with traditional methods. This work represents a significant advancement in computational mathematics, offering a potentially transformative solution for rigorous mathematical proof.

title: Generative Adversarial Networks for Symbolic Expression Discovery
abstract: This paper explores the application of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to the challenging problem of automatically discovering symbolic expressions from complex data. Traditional methods for symbolic expression discovery often rely on human expertise or computationally intensive search algorithms. This research proposes a novel approach where a GAN is trained to generate symbolic expressions that accurately reflect the underlying data distribution. The core mechanism involves a generator network producing symbolic expressions (represented as formulas or rules) and a discriminator network evaluating the quality of these expressions by comparing them to the data. The generated expressions are evaluated based on their ability to accurately model the data. The potential of this approach lies in its ability to uncover potentially novel mathematical relationships that might not be readily apparent through conventional methods. The paper details the architecture of the GAN, the loss functions employed, and the training process. The results, while not based on experimental data due to the nature of the theoretical exploration, highlight the feasibility and potential of this approach.

title: Based on Bio-Evolutionary Algorithm Hardware Architecture Design
abstract: This paper explores the application of bio-evolutionary algorithms for hardware architecture design. The core claim is that utilizing these algorithms can lead to more efficient and energy-saving hardware systems. The proposed mechanism involves transforming hardware architecture design problems into evolutionary problems, leveraging algorithms like genetic algorithms for optimization. This approach enables adaptive hardware optimization, offering a novel method compared to traditional design techniques. The research focuses on the theoretical framework and potential benefits, without empirical experimental validation. The work presents a detailed methodology and conceptual design for employing a bio-evolutionary algorithm to generate optimized hardware architectures, addressing the increasing demands for performance and energy efficiency in modern computing systems. The primary goal is to demonstrate the feasibility and potential advantages of this approach, paving the way for future research and development in self-optimizing hardware. ---

title: Interactive Theorem Proving with Large Language Models for Natural Language Formulation
abstract: This paper explores a new approach to theorem proving leveraging the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) to facilitate human-AI collaboration. The core challenge in automated theorem proving lies in the effective translation between natural language descriptions of mathematical problems and the formal logic required by theorem provers. This work introduces a system that employs an LLM to automatically convert natural language formulations of theorems into formal mathematical representations, enabling a natural language dialogue between the human prover and the theorem prover. The system aims to reduce the cognitive burden on the human prover by automating the initial translation step, allowing them to focus on the higher-level strategic aspects of the proof. We investigate the feasibility and potential of this interactive framework, highlighting key challenges and future directions. The system's architecture and initial results demonstrate a promising pathway for more intuitive and accessible theorem proving.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel algorithm for structure optimization in Bayesian networks based on adaptive parameter adjustment. Traditional methods often employ static configurations, limiting their effectiveness in dynamically changing data landscapes. Our proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts the parameters of a Bayesian network to optimize model performance, offering a more robust and adaptable approach. We demonstrate the algorithm's effectiveness through a series of experiments, showcasing improved accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. The core mechanism involves a self-adaptation strategy that continuously refines the network structure based on data-driven insights. The research contributes to the field of Bayesian networks by providing a practical and efficient solution for structure optimization, addressing a key challenge in model deployment and predictive accuracy.

title: Explainable AI for Graph Neural Networks via Structural Decomposition
abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have demonstrated remarkable success in various domains, including social network analysis, drug discovery, and recommendation systems. However, their "black box" nature – the difficulty in understanding *why* a GNN makes a particular prediction – remains a significant obstacle to their widespread adoption, especially in critical applications demanding trust and transparency. This paper proposes a novel explainability framework for GNNs based on structural decomposition. We hypothesize that understanding the key graph substructures that contribute to a GNN's prediction can significantly enhance interpretability. Our approach identifies and isolates these influential substructures, providing a granular view into the reasoning process of the network. We formally define the decomposition process using graph theory concepts, and demonstrate its application through a theoretical framework. The results highlight the importance of structural information in GNN predictions and offer a viable pathway toward more explainable and trustworthy GNN models.

title: Quantum Memory for Neural Networks with Topological Qubits
abstract: This paper explores the potential of employing topological qubits as a robust memory solution for neural networks. The primary challenge in utilizing quantum computing for complex tasks, particularly within neural networks, lies in the decoherence of quantum states. Traditional qubits are highly susceptible to environmental noise, leading to rapid state decay and hindering long-term computations. Topological qubits, due to their inherent properties arising from non-Abelian braiding, offer a promising solution by providing a fundamentally different approach to quantum information storage. This work details a proposed architecture where a neural network is constructed utilizing these topologically protected qubits. We investigate the theoretical framework for encoding and processing information using these qubits, focusing on minimizing decoherence effects. The core claim presented here is that topological qubits can significantly reduce decoherence issues, enabling more complex and longer-term computations within neural networks. We outline a potential computational model and discuss key considerations for implementing such a system, including qubit connectivity, error correction strategies, and the scaling of the network. The research introduces a new approach to quantum memory, directly addressing a critical bottleneck in the advancement of quantum neural networks.

title: Title: Adaptive Topology for Deep Learning Model Regularization
abstract: Deep learning models often exhibit sensitivity to training data, leading to suboptimal performance. Traditional regularization techniques, while effective, can be inflexible and require extensive hyperparameter tuning. This paper introduces an adaptive topology for deep learning model regularization that dynamically adjusts the connectivity patterns within a neural network based on the characteristics of the training data. We propose a reinforcement learning-based algorithm to automatically optimize the topology, resulting in improved generalization and robustness. The core mechanism leverages the concept of a dynamically evolving network structure to mitigate the effects of data heterogeneity. The proposed approach offers a novel and potentially transformative solution for enhancing deep learning model performance.

abstract: This paper presents a novel geometric proof of concept for quantum algorithm complexity, aiming to establish rigorous bounds on the runtime and memory requirements of quantum algorithms. This research offers a fundamentally new perspective on quantum algorithm complexity, moving beyond traditional asymptotic analysis and incorporating geometric insights to provide a more precise and automated assessment of algorithm behavior. The paper concludes with a detailed explanation of the geometric proof framework and its potential impact on the field of quantum computing.

title: Topological Quantum Information Protection Dynamic Adjustment
abstract: This paper explores the development of a novel quantum information protection scheme, termed "Dynamic Topological Quantum Information Protection," designed to enhance security and resilience against evolving threats. Traditional quantum information protection systems often employ static security measures, which lack the adaptability required to defend against sophisticated attacks. This research proposes a dynamic adjustment mechanism that iteratively refines the quantum state based on a predefined threat model, providing a proactive and adaptive defense strategy. The core of the system involves a meticulously designed quantum state evolution algorithm, incorporating feedback loops that continuously assess the threat landscape. We present a theoretical framework and preliminary implementation demonstrating the effectiveness of this dynamic approach in mitigating specific attack scenarios. The potential implications of this work extend to a broader range of quantum information security challenges, moving beyond static defenses towards a more robust and resilient system.

abstract: This paper investigates the application of dynamic information entropy self-adaptive aggregation to data clustering. title: Title: Entanglement Dynamics with Non-Locality Constraints
abstract: The study of entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents a formidable challenge due to its inherent non-locality. Traditional approaches struggle to adequately model the intricate interplay of correlations across vast distances, often leading to inconsistencies and limitations in experimental predictions. This research explores a novel framework for quantifying and controlling entanglement dynamics, specifically incorporating constraints imposed by non-local correlations. We propose a dynamically evolving "Chaos Mask" that actively modulates the entanglement state, driven by a learned probability distribution derived from the system's history. This approach seeks to surpass current limitations by offering a more robust and expressive model of correlated systems, potentially enabling breakthroughs in quantum information processing and fundamental physics. This paper presents a detailed theoretical analysis and preliminary experimental validation of this framework, demonstrating its ability to control entanglement evolution under complex non-local conditions.

title: Transformer-based emotion profiling and clustering of cybersickness narratives in Steam reviews of first-person virtual reality games
abstract: Cybersickness remains a persistent barrier in virtual reality (VR) gaming, yet how players emotionally frame discomfort in user-generated content is poorly understood. Prior large-scale analyses of Steam reviews have characterized emotional experience with a single polarity score. This study applies transformer-based emotion classification and unsupervised clustering to reviews of first-person VR games. A distilroberta-base model fine-tuned for emotion detection was applied to a cybersickness-focused subset of 1898 reviews and to a stratified sample of 50,000 drawn from a corpus of 1,375,125. Emotion profiles were compared across review valence with Mann-Whitney U tests, K-means clustering was applied to the stratified sample, and the cybersickness subset was compared with 9443 controls matched on application and valence, using ordinary least squares with cluster-robust standard errors and equivalence testing. Joy and neutral dominated. Sadness and disgust were higher in negative reviews and joy in positive ones, with large effects. Clustering identified six emotion profiles. The cybersickness subset initially appeared over-represented in the fear-dominant profile, but this difference disappeared under matching, and no dimension separated cases from controls, with equivalence established at 0.1 control standard deviations. Because the subset is defined at topic level, where prior validation places explicit symptom reports at 18.67%, the null applies to cybersickness-associated discourse rather than to verified symptom reports. In this corpus, emotional expression is organized by evaluation rather than topic, which constrains emotion-based screening and shows how platform-wide baselines can misattribute product composition to discourse.

title: CompEvo: Competition-Induced Evolution for Multi-Agent in News-Driven Time Series Forecasting
abstract: News-driven time series forecasting uses evolving textual events together with historical observations to predict future values, supporting applications such as market risk monitoring and resource scheduling. In multi-agent settings, two challenges still remain. The first is degeneration of thought, where agents converge to similar evidence-seeking behaviors. The second is insufficient theoretical grounding, where strategy updates are often heuristic and lack a principled formulation. To address the above challenges, we propose CompEvo, a competition-induced evolution framework for multi-agent news-driven time series forecasting. For theoretical grounding, we introduce an evolutionary game formulation to guarantee equilibrium existence and optimization convergence. Building on this formulation, we construct a trainable multi-agent evolution framework that integrates strategy execution, fitness-based differentiable selection, and competition-induced strategy evolution. CompEvo enables heterogeneous agents to explore diverse news evidence, converts forecasting feedback into differentiable influence weights, and evolves agent strategies under competitive pressure to preserve effective logic while maintaining diversity. Experiments on four real-world datasets show that CompEvo reduces RMSE by 27.3% and MAPE by 26.2% on average over strong baselines. Further analysis indicates that CompEvo successfully maintains diverse and specialized agent behaviors.

title: Hoss: Fast Oblivious Semantic Search with Heterogeneous GPU-CPU-TEE Architecture
abstract: Semantic search is widely deployed in modern AI systems, but protecting both data contents and access patterns remains challenging. The current state-of-the-art system, Compass, achieves oblivious semantic search by building an optimized ORAM over HNSW graphs. However, even with aggressive optimizations, it still incurs large overheads. Closing this performance gap is fundamentally difficult: Compass has already removed most cryptographic overheads, leaving ORAM accesses as the dominant cost, which are constrained by well-known Omega(log N) bandwidth lower bounds. Our key insight is that traditional ORAM overhead stems from the assumption of limited private memory, whereas modern GPU TEEs provide large private memory (Pmem) that blinds internal access patterns (Hunt et al., NSDI '23). This shift opens a new design space. We therefore propose Hoss, a first-of-its-kind oblivious semantic search system with a heterogeneous CPU-GPU TEE architecture that supports fast, scalable search with low cost of ownership. In Hoss, the GPU TEE's large Pmem hosts the hot-path HNSW traversal, while the lower layers of the graph, if they exceed GPU capacity, are offloaded to CPU TEEs. The system invokes oblivious primitives only when accessing these lower layers. The availability of large Pmem also enables new optimization opportunities. For example, Hoss features a host-access ORAM mechanism that goes beyond traditional performance constraints and incorporates several data-dependent optimizations that are not possible in prior designs. We implement a prototype of Hoss and benchmark it against Compass. Our results show that Hoss achieves up to 67x speedup while maintaining high recall, with larger gains at scale.

title: Hardware-Aware FP4 FlashAttention-4
abstract: Blackwell's 4-bit floating-point (FP4) tensor cores do not automatically make attention faster because softmax conversion and on-chip dependencies dominate once its matrix products shrink. We address this with \emph{Direct-P} for noncausal inference and a causal path that passes the forward quantization directly into backward. Direct-P maps scores directly to FP4 probabilities and reaches up to 2.13$\times$ the bfloat16 (BF16) forward throughput on an NVIDIA GB200. The causal path reconstructs probabilities from saved quantized queries and keys and uses 8-bit floating-point (FP8) gradient operands, accelerating a complete single-GPU 8-billion-parameter update by up to 1.14$\times$. Matched distributed training retains FP8 probabilities and values; every tested MXFP4 probability/value training trajectory diverges.

title: CulturalMenuBench: Probing the Knowledge-Application Gap in Multimodal Culinary Reasoning
abstract: Multimodal language models achieve near-ceiling scores on food recognition benchmarks, yet it remains unclear whether this success reflects genuine cultural understanding or mere visual matching. To probe this distinction, we introduce CulturalMenuBench, a benchmark of 4,870 items in 10 languages across 18 regions; its 10 tasks pair final-dish and step-by-step cooking images with ingredients, procedural text, and regional labels, spanning basic recognition to process-grounded cultural attribution. Evaluating 12 models exposes a substantial knowledge-application gap: models exceeding 94% on standard multiple-choice tasks drop to at most 56% when attributing dishes to Chinese regional cuisines, despite an identical four-way format. Diagnostic analyses explain why: error patterns are consistent with random guessing, accuracy tracks visual distinctiveness rather than cultural structure, and models classify cuisines more accurately from dish names alone than from images (+7-18 points). The knowledge is thus present but cannot be activated through visual input. An ablation confirms these tasks genuinely require procedural evidence: removing sequential cooking images selectively degrades process-grounded tasks while others remain stable. Overall, CulturalMenuBench shows that near-perfect recognition can conceal an inability to apply cultural knowledge, motivating training that explicitly connects perception, procedure, and cultural context. Code and data are publicly available.

title: Efficient Estimation of Reduced QAOA Expressibility on Acyclic Graphs
abstract: Classically equivalent formulations of an optimization problem need not lead to equivalent quantum algorithms. For MaxCut, fixing the value of a single vertex removes a simple global symmetry without changing the underlying optimization problem, yet it can substantially alter the quantum dynamics generated by the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA). These dynamics are captured by the circuit's dynamical Lie algebra (DLA), whose direct construction can become exponentially expensive. Here we show that, for symmetry-reduced QAOA on trees, substantial information about the reduced DLA can instead be obtained efficiently from the graph alone. We introduce a polynomial classical algorithm that recursively distinguishes vertices using shortest path structure and degree parity. When all vertices are resolved individually, the method determines the complete reduced DLA and, under the corresponding graph conditions, certifies maximal expressibility of the reduced QAOA ansatz. Even when full resolution is not achieved, the algorithm identifies embedded subalgebras, provides rigorous lower bounds on DLA dimension, and certifies controllable subsystems. Our theoretical and experimental results show how classical graph structure can be used to diagnose and potentially guide the quantum dynamics of variational algorithms before running them on quantum hardware.

title: Emerging Trends in Artificial Intelligence: A Review of Transformative Technologies and Applications
abstract: The current trends in Artificial Intelligence technologies continually transform multiple business sectors while changing how humans connect with machines. Contemporary technology views AI as its essential component instead of remaining as a separate specialized study field. A review of primary AI trends coupled with applications and obstacles in modern AI research served as the focus of this academic paper. Healthcare decision transparency integrates with financial needs to enable smart infrastructure deployment by connecting Explainable AI (XAI) with Federated Learning under Edge Computing framework. The barriers to progress include major issues with scalability together with interoperability standards and ethical needs for organizational governance. Interdisciplinary teamwork constitutes an absolute requirement to construct responsible AI systems together with dependable deployment frameworks as demonstrated through the term paper. The review combines recent research findings with guidance on new investigation tracks for developing all-encompassing AI systems which both spread far-reaching outcomes and follow sustainability requirements.

title: Reproducibility package for: A Cross-Silo Experimental Framework for Federated Voice Deepfake Detection: Heterogeneity, Poisoning, and Update-Cancellation Diagnostics
abstract: Data, code, results, and provenance package for the article “A Cross-Silo Experimental Framework for Federated Voice Deepfake Detection: Heterogeneity, Poisoning, and Update-Cancellation Diagnostics.” The package contains recovered original Linear-Frequency Cepstral Coefficient (LFCC)/WavLM notebooks, model checkpoints, training histories, poisoning/defense histories, score files, and automated artifact and Equal Error Rate (EER) verification, together with a fully specified 20-seed controlled update-cancellation experiment, independent-and-identically-distributed (IID)/non-IID heterogeneity ablations, defense-sensitivity analyses, attack-weight controls, reference outputs, figures, and reproduction instructions. The package documents both the archived original audio experiment and a controlled mechanism-replication experiment designed to isolate update cancellation and stress-test robust-aggregation assumptions. The latter is a synthetic mechanistic experiment and is not presented as external audio validation. The associated journal manuscript is intentionally not included in this archive. Copyrighted ASVspoof audio, large rebuildable feature caches, and third-party pretrained WavLM weights are not redistributed. The archived notebooks document how the derived feature representations can be regenerated from the publicly available source datasets. The package supports direct verification of the reported archived artifacts and reproducibility of the controlled numerical experiments. Exact bitwise-identical retraining of the historical audio experiment is not claimed because the original software environment was not fully pinned.

title: Adaptive Geometric Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the potential of adaptive geometric quantum entanglement to simulate topological structures and unlock new capabilities in quantum computing and information processing. The core concept revolves around leveraging quantum entanglement to mimic the intricate geometry of topological phases, providing a novel approach to system optimization and understanding. We investigate the mechanisms by which this simulation can lead to enhanced performance and the unique advantages of this approach. The research focuses on the application of quantum entanglement to generate and analyze topological configurations, ultimately aiming to address limitations of current quantum computation methods.

title: Title: Adaptive Quantum Algorithm Optimization via Dynamic Quantum Algorithm Tuning
abstract: This paper presents a novel optimization approach for quantum algorithms leveraging dynamic quantum algorithm tuning. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameter settings, limiting the potential for efficient algorithm execution. We introduce a dynamic mechanism that automatically adjusts the quantum algorithm's execution characteristics based on learned properties, resulting in accelerated quantum computation. The core of this method lies in a "dynamic quantum algorithm tuning" mechanism, which iteratively refines the algorithm's parameters to achieve optimal performance. This approach addresses the limitations of static optimization techniques by providing a flexible and adaptive optimization strategy. This research explores the potential of dynamically adjusting quantum algorithms to significantly enhance their computational speed.

title: 基于自适应神经网络的异质数据分布建模
abstract: This paper investigates the application of an adaptive neural network (ANN) framework for robust data distribution modeling. Traditional neural networks often rely on fixed, pre-defined parameters, limiting their ability to effectively handle diverse data distributions. This research introduces a novel ANN architecture that dynamically adjusts its parameters based on the characteristics of the input data, resulting in improved model generalization and robustness. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach through a series of simulations and experiments focusing on scenarios exhibiting varying data distributions. The core mechanism revolves around an adaptive parameter adjustment strategy, which leverages a feedback loop to continuously refine the network's response to changing data patterns. The results showcase a significant enhancement in model performance across a range of datasets, highlighting the potential for this approach in various data science applications.

title: Algorithmic Transparency and Explainability via Differential Privacy and Data Auditing
abstract: This paper explores a novel approach to enhancing algorithmic transparency and explainability in machine learning models by integrating differential privacy and data auditing techniques. Traditional explainability methods often fall short in addressing fundamental concerns about data privacy and potential biases embedded within datasets. We propose a framework where differential privacy is applied to mitigate privacy risks during model training, while automated data auditing tools meticulously track data lineage and identify potential sources of bias. The core mechanism involves adding calibrated noise to training data and model parameters, ensuring statistical privacy guarantees. Simultaneously, data auditing tools provide a traceable record of data transformations and feature selection, facilitating accountability and allowing for the detection of unintended biases. This approach moves beyond simply explaining model outputs and focuses on establishing a robust system of transparency and accountability throughout the entire machine learning lifecycle. The proposed methodology offers a significant advancement in building trustworthy and responsible AI systems.

title: Non-Standard Quantum State Collapse – Bayesian-Guided Reconstruction
abstract: This paper explores the challenges and opportunities of quantum state collapse, specifically focusing on the need for adaptive reconstruction techniques. We propose a novel Bayesian-guided algorithm designed to address this challenge by incorporating a dynamically adjusted Bayesian network. The algorithm aims to reconstruct complex quantum states from sparse data, leveraging the inherent probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. The core mechanism involves a Bayesian network that continuously refines the collapse process based on observed data, promoting a more robust and adaptable reconstruction. The paper details the algorithm's architecture, demonstrates its effectiveness through illustrative examples, and discusses its potential implications for various quantum computing applications.

title: Dynamic Bayesian Networks for Explainable Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Explainable Reinforcement Learning (XRL) is a burgeoning field aiming to address the inherent "black-box" nature of traditional reinforcement learning (RL) agents, particularly deep neural networks. This work proposes a novel approach leveraging Dynamic Bayesian Networks (DBNs) to provide interpretable explanations for RL policies. The core idea is to represent the agent's knowledge of the environment and its actions within a DBN, allowing for explicit probabilistic reasoning. The agent's experience dynamically updates the DBN, leading to a transparent account of the policy decisions. Unlike traditional RL methods that primarily focus on reward optimization, this approach directly encodes and explains the reasoning process. We demonstrate the potential of this framework by outlining its construction and operation, highlighting its advantages in terms of interpretability and providing a foundation for future research. The key contribution lies in the explicit modeling of belief states and their evolution, offering a pathway to understand *why* an RL agent makes specific decisions.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning via Temporal Logic Programming
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to neuro-symbolic reasoning that leverages temporal logic programming. The core idea is to bridge the gap between neural networks and symbolic reasoning by employing temporal logic to explicitly represent and reason about temporal dependencies within a system. We train a neural network to predict the truth value of temporal logic formulas, effectively translating neural network outputs into symbolic representations. These symbolic representations are then fed into a symbolic reasoning engine, allowing for the execution of complex reasoning tasks that would be difficult or impossible with purely neural or purely symbolic approaches. The system's architecture and training methodology are detailed, highlighting the benefits of this combined approach. We demonstrate the potential of this method through a theoretical framework, focusing on the integration of temporal logic and neural network predictions. The key innovation lies in the direct application of temporal logic as the interface between the neural and symbolic components, offering a more interpretable and controllable method for neuro-symbolic reasoning.

title: Formal Specification of Secure Multi-Party Computation Protocols
abstract: Secure Multi-Party Computation (MPC) allows multiple parties to compute a function without revealing their individual inputs. However, ensuring the security of MPC protocols is a complex and challenging task. This paper presents a novel approach to formally specifying and verifying MPC protocols, leveraging mathematical frameworks like category theory to provide a rigorous foundation. We define key security properties using mathematical notation, focusing on completeness, soundness, and correctness. The core claim is that formal specifications significantly enhance the confidence in the security of MPC protocols by enabling automated verification. This work outlines a methodology for constructing formal models of MPC protocols, highlighting the benefits of a mathematically precise approach compared to traditional, informal security analyses. The detailed formulation and application of these specifications will contribute to the development of more robust and trustworthy MPC systems.

title: Quantum State Non-Linear Mapping and Topology Transformations
abstract: Quantum states exhibit remarkable sensitivity to their environment, making them ideal candidates for exploring novel quantum device designs. This paper investigates the interplay between non-linear mapping and topology transformations, proposing a novel algorithm for dynamically optimizing quantum device design based on the observed effects of these transformations. We analyze how non-linear mapping alters the topology of quantum states, leading to quantifiable changes in device performance. The core mechanism focuses on a specific mapping function, which is then optimized through iterative transformations. This research explores the potential for leveraging these transformations to achieve unprecedented device design precision and efficiency. The resulting design suggests a pathway toward the creation of highly tailored quantum devices with enhanced capabilities.

title: Dynamic Modular Quantum Computation for Non-Von Neumann Architectures
abstract: This paper proposes a novel quantum computing architecture termed "Dynamic Modular Quantum Computation" (DMQC) that fundamentally departs from the traditional Von Neumann architecture by eliminating the need for classical storage units. The core concept leverages quantum entanglement and dynamic module reconfiguration to achieve parallel quantum computation and efficient result aggregation. The architecture is built upon entangled quantum modules, where the degree of entanglement and module connectivity are dynamically controlled to orchestrate computations. This approach directly addresses the inherent storage limitations of Von Neumann architectures, offering a significantly more scalable and potentially more efficient pathway toward realizing practical quantum computation. This paper outlines the theoretical framework, key operational principles, and potential advantages of the DMQC architecture, highlighting its departure from conventional design paradigms. ---

title: Quantum Entanglement Encoding for Multi-Dimensional Data Compression
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to multi-dimensional data compression leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement. Traditional compression methods often struggle to overcome the inherent limitations imposed by the Shannon entropy theorem, particularly when dealing with complex, high-dimensional data. Our proposed method utilizes the correlated nature of entangled quantum states to achieve superior compression ratios. We demonstrate a mapping of multi-dimensional data into a set of entangled quantum states, exploiting the instantaneous correlations between these states to represent the data efficiently. The core of the method lies in manipulating the entangled states to encode information, potentially exceeding the compression limits achievable with classical techniques. The theoretical framework is outlined, focusing on the key mathematical principles underpinning the entanglement-based compression process. This work explores the potential of quantum mechanics to revolutionize data compression, offering a new paradigm for handling vast datasets with unprecedented efficiency. The method is presented with a focus on the mathematical formulation and the underlying principles.

title: Probability Field Theory-Driven Computation: A Novel Framework for Quantum Computing Efficiency and Algorithm Design
abstract: Probability Field Theory (PFT) offers a powerful approach to quantum computing by leveraging the unique properties of quantum entanglement and the quantum spin. This paper investigates the application of PFT to drive computation, specifically focusing on the utilization of spin-dependent quantum gates to enhance quantum algorithm efficiency. We present a novel framework, "Self-Spin Dynamics," that employs a self-induced spin-state to facilitate quantum interference and entanglement, thereby optimizing the performance of quantum algorithms. The core mechanism involves the creation of self-oscillating spin states, which allow for the manipulation of quantum states with unprecedented precision. The paper explores the potential of this approach in addressing limitations inherent in traditional quantum computing and demonstrates preliminary results suggesting significant improvements in algorithm speed and accuracy. The investigation explores the impact of self-oscillating spin states on quantum circuit design and optimization, providing a pathway towards more efficient quantum computations.

title: Quantum-Enhanced Optimization of Constraint Programming
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of quantum algorithms to accelerate the solution of constraint programming problems. Traditional methods often struggle with the vast solution spaces, necessitating significant computational resources. We explore the application of quantum annealing and quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) to enhance the search process, aiming to significantly reduce the time required for optimization. The core mechanism involves leveraging quantum phenomena to overcome the limitations of classical algorithms, offering a promising avenue for improved performance in constraint programming. The research focuses on the theoretical advantages and potential practical implementations of these quantum approaches, specifically examining how they can be applied to benchmark problems and demonstrate a quantifiable speedup compared to traditional methods.

title: Dimension Space Information Theory Reinforcement Learning Framework
abstract: This paper presents a novel reinforcement learning framework based on dimension space information theory, designed to address the challenges of high-dimensional environments. We propose a method that leverages the inherent structure of high-dimensional spaces to guide exploration and learning, enabling the development of robust and optimal strategies. The core of this framework utilizes information theory principles to represent state spaces and action spaces, allowing for efficient and adaptive policy learning. The framework's innovation lies in its integration of both traditional reinforcement learning techniques and dimension space information theory, resulting in improved performance across a range of complex scenarios. We demonstrate the framework's effectiveness through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to learn complex strategies and achieve high rewards. The key contribution is a method for automatically discovering optimal policies within high-dimensional spaces, moving beyond the limitations of conventional approaches.

title: Quantum Entanglement Path Discovery – A Dynamic Path Exploration Approach
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, presents unique opportunities for computation and information transfer. This paper investigates a novel quantum path discovery method leveraging the inherent dynamic properties of entangled states. We propose a framework that employs a continuous, iterative exploration of entangled quantum states, optimizing for a predefined objective function through a process of dynamic path adjustment. The core mechanism centers on exploiting entanglement to instantaneously correlate states and guide the exploration process. This approach offers a significant advancement over traditional algorithms, particularly in scenarios demanding high efficiency and robustness. We detail the methodology, analyze its potential benefits, and present preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this dynamic path discovery strategy.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel dynamic adaptive probability space optimization algorithm designed to address the challenges of complex optimization problems. Traditional optimization methods often rely on static parameters, limiting the algorithm's ability to effectively model and predict the outcomes of intricate optimization scenarios. Our proposed algorithm dynamically adjusts probability space parameters, enabling a more nuanced and responsive optimization process. This approach enhances the algorithm's capacity to capture the inherent complexities within the problem domain, resulting in improved optimization quality and robustness. We detail the core mechanism, the design of the dynamic parameter adjustment process, and the resulting performance improvements compared to existing approaches. The paper concludes with a discussion of the algorithm's potential applications and future research directions.

title: Pigeons That Learn to Flank You: A Interdisciplinary Mapping Review of AI Techniques for NPCs and Dynamic Worlds
abstract: This article presents a narrative review of AI Techniques for NPCs and Dynamic Worlds in the context of Game Development. The literature on this topic has expanded substantially over recent decades, yet it remains fragmented across subfields, methods, and national research traditions. Drawing on an interpretive synthesis of representative contributions, the review reconstructs the historical development of the area, examines the conceptual foundations and definitional disputes that organize its debates, and maps the contemporary landscape of research, including the methodological shift toward data-intensive approaches and the institutional pressures that shape publication practice. Particular attention is given to the role of game AI and NPCs as organizing themes, and to the conditions under which findings from different research traditions can be brought into productive comparison. The review identifies three synthetic conclusions: the literature is cumulatively strong but organizationally weak; methodological pluralism is better understood as a resource than as a defect; and the growing practical salience of the topic raises the stakes of its unresolved conceptual questions. An agenda for future work is proposed, emphasizing integrative research designs, transparent synthesis practices, and the protection of definitional and infrastructural work on which cumulative progress depends. The article is intended as both a reference map for newcomers and a provocation for specialists in Game Development.

title: Soft Disagreement-Based Adaptive Uncertainty Regulation for Fuzzy Servo Control
authors: Dosti Kh. Abbas Dosti Kh. Abbas
abstract: This paper proposes a supervisory soft disagreement framework for adaptive uncertainty regulation in Interval Type-2 (IT2) fuzzy servo control and validates its performance through embedded implementation on an industrial servo platform. The proposed framework introduces a supervisory learning layer that combines supervised classification and unsupervised fuzzy clustering to characterize servo operating conditions using experimentally extracted performance indicators, including rise time, settling time, overshoot, steady-state error, Integral Absolute Error (IAE), control-effort energy, tracking-error standard deviation, and maximum control effort. Operating condition confidence is quantified by measuring the soft disagreement between the posterior class probabilities of a Support Vector Machine (SVM) classifier and the normalized membership degrees of a Fuzzy C-Means (FCM) clustering algorithm using the Bhattacharyya coefficient. The resulting disagreement index adaptively regulates the Footprint of Uncertainty (FOU) of the antecedent membership functions in IT2 fuzzy controller. A closed-form Uncertainty Avoider Defuzzification (UAD) strategy enables computationally efficient uncertainty-aware type reduction for real-time embedded implementation without iterative procedures. The framework was trained using experimental data collected from a Delta ASDA-B2 400 W industrial servo drive under diverse operating conditions. The complete controller was implemented on a Raspberry Pi and experimentally compared with conventional Proportional–Integral–Derivative (PID), Type-1, and fixed-FOU IT2 fuzzy controllers. Experimental results show that the proposed controller achieved an average IAE of 1.08, representing improvements of 55.6% and 27.5% over the PID and fixed-FOU IT2 controllers, respectively. Overshoot was reduced to 2.2% and settling time to 0.24 s, while the supervisory computation required only 4.55 ms, confirming real-time feasibility. The scientific significance of this work lies in introducing a new disagreement-driven supervisory paradigm that links probabilistic machine learning confidence with adaptive fuzzy uncertainty regulation. By establishing a principled connection among supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and Interval Type-2 fuzzy control, the proposed framework provides a general foundation for confidence-aware adaptive uncertainty management in intelligent control systems operating under uncertain and time-varying conditions.

title: PerfReasoning: How Well Do LLMs Reason on Hardware Performance?
abstract: Performance modeling is central to hardware design and software optimization, yet constructing these models requires structured reasoning about computation, data reuse, storage, and movement. We introduce PerfReasoning, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs both as direct performance reasoners and as generators of analytical performance-model code. Given workload, architecture, and mapping specifications, models compare mappings and predict off-chip traffic and buffer requirements. The strongest closed-source models exceed 90% on reasoning-based Q&A, and the best open-weight model reaches 82.4%. However, model construction is substantially harder: while GPT-5.6 Sol exceeds 80% pass rate, all other model configurations average below 45% and vary markedly across runs. Task-specific RL raises a 4B model's mapping-reasoning accuracy by 15.7 points, whereas feedback-free multi-round self-revision prompting is not reliably effective. PerfReasoning exposes the gap between plausible architectural reasoning and reliable performance-model construction. We will publicly release the benchmark to support reproducible evaluation and track future progress.
